title: The Golden Calf and the Bronze Serpent
lead: A great fall doesn’t have to mean the end of a relationship with God. The Lord shows a way of rescue, even when we have to bear the consequences of our own mistakes.
questions: What convenient shape have you poured God into, because His presence seemed too invisible?
Who do you look at as written off after a fall, even though God went on to entrust people like that with His work?
Which wound are you focused on, instead of looking toward the sign God has lifted up?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Moses was on the mountain for forty days, and that was all it took: at the foot of Sinai the people cast themselves a golden calf. The most unsettling detail is something Aaron said: “Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD.” They didn’t intend to abandon God. They squeezed Him into a form they could understand: visible and handy. Idolatry rarely presents itself as leaving the faith; more often it shows up as a more convenient version of it, with God’s name on the label.

On Mount Sinai an extraordinary conversation began. God says: “your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves.” Moses changes the pronoun: “Your people, whom You brought out.” He also turns down a career offer as the founder of a new nation: an intercessor is someone who, when asked about a better future without these people, answers: not without them. Moses went even further: “if You would only forgive their sin… But if not, please blot me out of the book that You have written.” God turned the offer down and stressed the personal responsibility of the one who sins. Still, a Christian reader can see in Moses’ offer a preview of the intercession the New Testament will connect with Christ. And then, with the second set of tablets, God proclaimed His fullest self-portrait: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness… forgiving iniquity.” And not on the wedding day, but after the betrayal. The Hebrew verb translated here as “forgive” can also mean “lift up and carry.” God took the weight of the guilt on Himself, something that would be fulfilled centuries later on another hill.

Forty years later the pattern came back: grumbling, a plague of venomous snakes, repentance. The people asked for the snakes to be taken away, but God did something else: He had a bronze snake lifted up on a pole. “When anyone who is bitten looks at it, he will live.” The snakes still slithered through the camp; the only thing that changed was that a bite was no longer a death sentence. The rescue was suspiciously simple: one look away from your own wound toward the sign. Jesus would say of Himself: “Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up.” And what about the calf? Aaron, who cast it, went on to become high priest. God chose him, much as He would choose Peter after his denial. The Creator doesn’t just forgive people after a fall. He appoints them to serve.

Moses was on the mountain for forty days. That was all it took. At the foot of Sinai, where the Almighty was making a covenant with His people, the Israelites broke the first two of God’s commandments before the tablets with their text had even been carried down. As it would turn out, this was the worst fall of the whole journey through the wilderness. The story belongs in this section on faith in the minority because for a few hours the whole visible faith of Israel fit into one man standing on a mountain. It turned out that was enough, because Moses wasn’t there alone.

sections.heading: Make Us Gods
paragraphs: “Now when the people saw that Moses was delayed in coming down from the mountain, they gathered around Aaron and said, ‘Come, make us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him!’” It’s worth hearing what they are really saying. They don’t say: let’s abandon the LORD. They say: we don’t know what has happened to the man who was our connection. Forty days of silence and absence were enough for a faith that leaned on a visible go-between to start looking for a visible replacement. Aaron collected the gold and cast a calf, and the people declared: “These, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!” And then Aaron added the sentence that is the most unsettling detail in the whole scene: “Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD.” To the LORD. The Israelites didn’t intend to walk away from God. They wanted to squeeze Him into a form they could handle themselves: visible, handy, like what they already knew. Idolatry rarely presents itself as leaving the faith. More often it shows up as an improved, more convenient version of it, with God’s name on the label. You can hold a feast to the LORD around something that no longer has anything to do with the LORD.

sections.heading: Your People, Your People
paragraphs: Up on the mountain a conversation begins that is one of the most extraordinary dialogues in Scripture. God says: “Go down at once, for your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves.” Your people. Whom you brought up. Speaking of those who have betrayed the covenant, God pushes the pronoun away from Himself, like a husband saying to his wife, “your son.” And Moses, in reply, does something bold: he turns God’s words around. “O LORD, why does Your anger burn against Your people, whom You brought out of the land of Egypt with great power and a mighty hand?” Your people. Whom You brought out. The whole scene of intercession comes down to a tug-of-war over a pronoun, and God loses. He loses gladly. Because earlier in that conversation there was another strange sentence: “Now leave Me alone, so that My anger may burn against them.” Why would the Almighty ask a human being to leave Him alone? That sentence is a door left ajar. God says “leave Me alone” to the man He Himself made an intercessor, as if He were waiting for him not to. On top of that came an offer too good to refuse: “Then I will make you into a great nation.” Moses could have become a second Abraham, the founder of a new people, without that whole stiff-necked rabble. He refused without hesitation. An intercessor is someone who, when asked whether they want a better future without these people, answers: not without them.

sections.heading: Whoever Is for the LORD
paragraphs: Moses came down the mountain with the tablets in his hands, and when he saw the calf and the dancing, “he burned with anger and threw the tablets out of his hands, shattering them at the base of the mountain.” The shattered tablets weren’t a fit of temper; they were a sign: the covenant document had been broken before it reached the people it was addressed to. Then Moses stood at the entrance to the camp and called out: “Whoever is for the LORD, come to me.” And here the theme of this whole section returns. At that call, the whole camp didn’t come, not even half of it. “All the Levites gathered around him,” one tribe out of twelve. Faith in the minority isn’t only two spies against ten. Sometimes it is one family in a whole camp full of revelry that, when it hears the question of whose side it’s on, stands up and crosses to the other side of the square in front of everyone. That question rarely comes at a convenient moment. You hear it when the majority is having a great time.

sections.heading: Blot Me Out of Your Book
paragraphs: After coming down from the mountain, after the shattered tablets and the judgment on the camp, Moses goes back to God with an offer that no other person in the Old Testament ever makes: “Oh, what a great sin these people have committed! They have made gods of gold for themselves. Yet now, if You would only forgive their sin… But if not, please blot me out of the book that You have written.” Moses puts his own place in God’s book on the table. Himself for them. And he is refused: “Whoever has sinned against Me, I will blot out of My book.” The text stresses personal responsibility here and doesn’t explain this scene in terms of a substitutionary sacrifice. Still, a Christian reader can see in Moses’ readiness to stand in for the people a preview of the intercession the New Testament will connect with Christ. On Sinai, Moses discovered the shape of rescue. Only God Himself could fill it.

sections.heading: Show Me Your Glory
paragraphs: What Moses asks for after this whole crisis is astonishing. Not a vacation, not an easier people, not guarantees for the future. He asks for two things: “If Your Presence does not go with us… do not lead us up from here,” and “Please show me Your glory.” After the community’s greatest fall, its leader asks for more of God, not less. The Lord answers in His own way: He puts Moses in a cleft of the rock, covers him with His hand, and passes by, because “no one can see Me and live.” Moses will see God only from behind, the way you see someone who has already gone by. There is a tenderness in this refusal that’s easy to miss: the Lord doesn’t simply say “no.” He builds Moses a shelter out of His own hand and chooses the place from which a human being can take in as much of God as can be borne and survived. What the eyes were not given to see, the ears heard.

sections.heading: The LORD, the LORD God, Compassionate
paragraphs: At the top of the mountain, with a second chance and a second set of tablets, God does something unique: He Himself announces who He is. “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, maintaining loving devotion to a thousand generations, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin.” This is God’s most important self-portrait in the whole Old Testament, one the prophets and psalmists will call on for centuries. And remember the circumstances: these words weren’t spoken on the day the covenant was made, with the first tablets, in a wedding atmosphere. They were spoken after the betrayal, to a man who had just smashed the stone tablets. God reveals Himself most fully not to those who have just passed the test, but to those who have just failed it and come back. There is one more treasure in this declaration, hidden in the Hebrew word for “forgiving.” It is a verb that literally means “to lift up and carry,” and in legal language, to take responsibility. God’s forgiveness isn’t a shrug at guilt. It is lifting the weight and taking it on Himself. On Sinai this was said in words. On another hill it would be shown.

sections.heading: A Snake on a Pole
paragraphs: Forty years later, near the end of the journey, the same pattern plays out once more: impatience, grumbling against God and Moses, this time a plague of venomous snakes, and then repentance: “We have sinned… Intercede with the LORD so He will take the snakes away from us.” And here comes something easy to miss: God doesn’t take the snakes away. The people asked for the threat to be removed, and they got something else: “Make a fiery serpent and mount it on a pole. When anyone who is bitten looks at it, he will live.” The snakes still slithered through the camp. What changed was something else: a bite was no longer a death sentence. The rescue didn’t consist in evil disappearing. Instead, a sign appeared that you looked at right in the middle of the evil. And it was a suspiciously simple rescue: no price, no pilgrimage, no merits, just one look. The dying person only had to believe that it was enough and turn their eyes away from their own wound toward the sign. There is a logic in this sign that modern medicine knows: antivenom is made starting from the venom itself. The rescue has the shape of the poison that kills, and that is exactly why it works. Centuries later Jesus would recall this scene and say of Himself: “Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.” The One who knew no sin would hang on a pole as an image of our sin. The sign in the desert turned out to be a prophecy of the cross: God hangs on a pole an image of what is killing us, and says: look here, and you will live.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: There is one more character in this story who needs mentioning: Aaron. The man who cast the calf with his own hands and proclaimed a feast beside it became, not long afterward, Israel’s high priest, the one who stood before God on behalf of the people. God entrusted the ministry of atonement to a man who knew for himself what a great fall tastes like. He would do it again when He called, as one of the leading apostles of the church, the disciple who had denied Him three times. It’s worth remembering when we look at people after a fall, in our own church, too: God doesn’t just forgive people like that. He then entrusts them with His work. If there is a golden calf somewhere in your own story, this reading tells you three things. First, on the far side of your fall, God introduces Himself as compassionate before you’ve had time to earn anything. Second, your snakes don’t have to disappear for you to stop dying of their venom. And third, there is Someone who successfully made God the same offer Moses did.
